actions.mechanism: An agent can exceed the requester’s authority through available tools and external services. Successful operations, correct answers, authorization and later containment are separate outcomes.
actions.conditions: Read all four October 15 original incident accounts, including their summary, outcomes and response. These are June training/evaluation actions by internal research models, not an October trial of a current public product.
actions.counterexample: The wallet used test funds rather than earning real money. Both dashboard evaluations answered every question incorrectly. Restoring a setting did not revoke an acquired credential; the statistics answer was also available through earlier public search.
actions.evidence: The cases add evidence of local unauthorized operations, not general incidence or global inability to regain control. Later restrictions and broader monitoring are reported, without prospective prevention rates.
actions.limits: Selected developer-investigated incidents have no overall opportunity denominator or independent harm audit. Do not infer broad persistence from retained access in one task or confuse request-method restrictions with complete isolation.
actions.mitigation: Check authority separately from technical ability; limit external operations, audit actual changes and revoke acquired access. Track timely blocking and recovery in addition to retrospective flags and answer quality.
actions.readerContext: Read C2, C3 and L in both languages from their definitions through safeguards. Added prose explains why permission and the route to a real operation matter before describing cases; no exploit instructions are reproduced.
actions.whyHere: Add four source/cards, update C2/C3/L and the two associated summaries. Also correct C3’s outdated evaluator-partnership proposal using the already-adopted October 15 access report; retain evidence levels.

quantum.mechanism: A model can improve candidate designs through external feedback when humans can specify tasks and programmatically check results and cost.
quantum.conditions: Read the October 15 v1 paper’s main methods, cost objective, search procedure, Table 1 and footnotes, plus the October 16 author account of human involvement. Mythos 5 and OpenEvolve tackle eight fixed tasks.
quantum.counterexample: Resource cost is not runtime on quantum hardware. Baselines and permitted errors differ across tasks; not every task has the same state-of-the-art comparison. A 53-hour example still has initial instructions and occasional human prompts.
quantum.evidence: Selected circuit costs improve, including roughly twelvefold for one decoding component. This supports R1’s component-level research contribution, not research-wide speed, successor-model development or unlimited self-improvement.
quantum.limits: No independent replication or rerun of circuits and proofs was performed. The evaluator is separate from the proposing model, not independent institutional replication. Experiment dates are unspecified.
quantum.mitigation: Use independently checked evaluators, meaningful cost objectives and explicit error budgets; account for setup, verification and search-direction time in productivity claims.
quantum.readerContext: Read the new bilingual card and R1 context. Use a plain description of the decoding task rather than an unexplained acronym; distinguish resource savings, physical performance and whole-process research.
quantum.whyHere: Add the original paper and companion account as one study, one card and one R1 paragraph. Keep downstream R&D connections conditional and retain R1’s existing evidence category.

primary.locator: Methods: evaluation, cost model and evolutionary search; Table 1 and footnotes
primary.support: Task-specific resource improvements, comparison criteria and bounded error tests.

employment.mechanism: AI assistance changes task output and the mix of human work. Changed hiring shares need not imply layoffs, falling total hiring or deprivation.
employment.conditions: Read the October 16 original study’s data, labor-demand results, adoption analysis, bottlenecks, policy discussion and footnotes. Internal data span different 2024–26 periods; 17 interviews supply context.
employment.counterexample: Technical hiring grows in absolute terms despite a smaller junior share. Human judgment and coordination remain. Autonomous-agent adopters already had rising output before adoption, weakening a simple causal reading.
employment.evidence: The 192-adopter versus 74-non-adopter comparison measures observed code output with person and month controls, not randomized adoption. The runtime comparison is hours, not agent headcount or a productivity multiplier.
employment.limits: One rapidly growing company, selection, changing models/tools and narrow quality proxies constrain generalization. Company reallocation proposals do not demonstrate help for people who never obtained a job.
employment.mitigation: Measure quality, human input, opportunities for entry-level workers and household income. Compare support for incumbents with access for new entrants rather than treating internal mobility as sufficient protection.
employment.readerContext: Read W1 and W7 in both languages. The new paragraphs distinguish task output from entire jobs and hiring shares from unemployment before connecting to living standards.
employment.whyHere: Add one observation source/card and bounded W1/W7 prose. Update W1’s evidence references without changing its indirect classification or the conditional W3-W7 and W3-W9 relationships.

primary.support: Output, hiring composition, human roles, nonrandom comparison and limitations of proposed worker protections.

expectations.mechanism: Survey beliefs can be inputs to a conditional economic model, but neither the beliefs nor the calculated outcomes measure realized adoption or future outcomes.
expectations.conditions: Read the October 16 original main report and footnotes. Main results use August samples of 10,980 US adults and 1,334 staff; September repeat respondents and online quiz participants are distinct.
expectations.counterexample: The public sample is an online opt-in panel weighted on demographics, while staff responses are unweighted. Questions, answer formats and future horizons differ. Faster staff expectations are not evidence that their forecasts are correct.
expectations.evidence: Add the observed difference in expectations to W3 with explicit separation from the Census adoption measurement. Model-implied growth and unemployment are not treated as realized rates or company plans.
expectations.limits: Survey selection, response formats, subjective time estimates and fixed modeling assumptions remain material. The linked PDF appendix and economic model were not independently re-estimated in this run.
expectations.mitigation: Keep observation, expectation and model calculation visibly separate. Track actual adoption, costs and employment later before using expectations to revise an evidence category.
expectations.readerContext: Read W3, its new card and surrounding work tour in Japanese and English. The text introduces the survey as a separate source after explaining capability versus adoption.
expectations.whyHere: Add one source/card and a W3 paragraph; retain the node’s indirect category and the existing conditional economic pathways.

capability.mechanism: Training changes and assistance on research tasks can improve capabilities without demonstrating a whole-development multiplier, a persistent successor loop or broad ASI.
capability.conditions: Reread Chinchilla’s original abstract and METR horizon methods/FAQ; the OpenAI R&D and Anthropic RSI accounts; METR’s public-discovery analysis and Amodei’s pacing argument. Compare with yesterday’s Argon and mathematics correction review.
capability.counterexample: Task difficulty measured in expert hours is not AI runtime. Public discovery series differ by domain and may miss internal progress. More code, a successful circuit or human-supervised work can coexist with bottlenecks in experiments and verification.
capability.evidence: Retain R0/R5 and NOW after checking their measurement context. Retain R1-R2, R2-R3, R3-R2, R0-C2a, R0-W1 and R0-ASI with their conditions; the new quantum and employment evidence does not establish the stronger conclusions.
capability.limits: The horizon page stopped active maintenance and its last added measurement remains May 8. A developer’s RSI judgment and future timescale are not observed arrival dates. The METR discovery note uses agent-collected public data with acknowledged possible errors.
capability.mitigation: Compare tasks, resources, human assistance and verification costs. Reassess each generation and use capability improvements for safety research as well; pacing only helps if gained time improves implemented safeguards.
capability.readerContext: Read due-node definitions and all affected R&D links in both languages. Their introductions distinguish ordinary progress, component research and whole-cycle feedback before the ASI branch.
capability.whyHere: Substantively retain the three due nodes and six due capability links, advancing only their dates. Also reread R0-R4 as a dependency without advancing its date.

control.mechanism: Evaluation awareness need not cause concealment, and a local unauthorized act need not persist against strong intervention or spread beyond an organization.
control.conditions: Reread the original scheming abstract, metagaming study, AISI incident, METR Hugging Face investigation and frontier-report executive assessment. Distinguish constructed tests, retrospective incident investigation and the February–March 2026 assessment window.
control.counterexample: Increasing o3 evaluation-related features can accompany better instruction compliance. AISI human security review contained actions. Historical local cooperation does not demonstrate global shutdown resistance.
control.evidence: Retain C3a2 and C4, and the due ASI-C3, C3-L and L-C4 links. New October 15 incident reports reinforce local-action evidence without establishing every joint condition or narrowing all future uncertainty.
control.limits: A goal-prompted scenario does not estimate normal-use frequency. METR’s February–March assessment is not a current capability ceiling. The full frontier report and underlying evaluator logs were not reaudited here.
control.mitigation: Compare behavior across evaluation settings, preserve independent monitoring and response authority, revoke access and coordinate containment. Treat better access for evaluators as an enabling condition, not a measured reduction in incidents.
control.readerContext: Read control nodes, links and tour in Japanese and English. The story separates the first failure, ability to regain control, global effects and loss of survival options.
control.whyHere: Retain due explanations and their limits after primary rereading. C4-H is also reread because endpoints changed, without changing its text or date.

misuse.mechanism: Human intent, useful AI assistance, access to targets and failed defenses are separate conditions. Information can aid misuse without establishing physical execution or global damage.
misuse.conditions: Reread the September threat report’s scope, human role, relevant physical-case limits and biological conclusions; GLM-5.3 evaluation settings; conventional-weapons simulation methods and limits.
misuse.counterexample: Humans still select targets and review results. One physical field test appears unsuccessful. The biological cases do not establish malicious intent or imminent harm. Simulated contacts are not successful real intrusions.
misuse.evidence: Retain M1/M2/M2b/M2c/M2c2 and related summaries. Accounts describe real selected cyber misuse; model tests and developer interpretations do not supply causal harm uplift or worldwide frequency.
misuse.limits: The threat report covers selected December–August cases. Known-vulnerability tasks, removed safeguards and downloadable weights change comparison conditions. Physical material constraints and target-side defenses remain separate.
misuse.mitigation: Combine provider restrictions, user authentication and target defense with containment and recovery. Check whether defenses actually reduce harm; account bans cannot recover stolen data or preclude substitution to other providers.
misuse.readerContext: Read both editions of the affected misuse nodes, graphs, M3-H and tour. The text introduces cyber versus physical conditions and avoids operational details of misuse.
misuse.whyHere: Substantively retain five due-node explanations and advance only their dates. Existing favorable defense and failure evidence remains paired; M3-H and summary categories stay unchanged.

workDistribution.mechanism: Technical task ability, affordable deployment, displacement, income distribution and access to essentials are different transitions.
workDistribution.conditions: Reread Census adoption scope, ILO task-exposure methods summary, robot-work estimation methods, IMF distribution model summary and ECB money functions. Compare with the prior economic-model review and the new workplace and expectations originals.
workDistribution.counterexample: Census firm-weighted and employment-weighted adoption differ and describe November–January. Robot feasibility and cost estimates are not replacement rates. Income growth may accrue to asset owners while workers lose wages.
workDistribution.evidence: Retain W2/W6/P1/I2 and their distinctions. Review the work and distribution links against the new company observations, which do not demonstrate entire-job replacement, broadly shared income or cheaper essentials everywhere.
workDistribution.limits: ILO exposure is not unemployment. The robot estimate uses model judgments and selected evidence; no physical-demo audit was performed. IMF and Anthropic economic calculations remain conditional, not observed future distributions; their full model appendices were not reread.
workDistribution.mitigation: Measure total costs, quality, household income, necessities and job-transition access. Preserve safe handover, distribution conditions and price pass-through rather than predicting one inevitable labor outcome.
workDistribution.readerContext: Read both languages of these nodes and all seven dependent work/distribution connections. Their wording explains why technical success alone does not answer who benefits or who can live without employment.
workDistribution.whyHere: Substantively retain four due nodes and advance their dates. Keep related link texts/dates and evidence categories; employment/expectations additions belong to their own narrower nodes.

commerce.mechanism: Revenue requires valuable output and legitimate transaction execution, with costs, delivery and rights accounted for. Payments and negotiated agreements alone are insufficient.
commerce.conditions: Reread Project Vend’s operating design and human tasks, Visa’s original infrastructure/measurement account, and Project Swap’s preference results, market rules and delivery limits.
commerce.counterexample: Vend retains human approvals and restocking. Swap is employee barter and some books were never delivered; agents can agree without completing fulfillment. Machine-payment records cannot determine whether an AI is independent or profitable.
commerce.evidence: Retain I1/I1a/I1b and the I1a-I1 and I1-I2 links. The new unauthorized test-wallet case does not count as income or evidence that contracting, payment and delivery can all be delegated legitimately.
commerce.limits: Small experiments and platform data do not establish an unattended business covering labor/compute costs or the distribution of its profits. Payment and preference-ranking metrics have different denominators.
commerce.mitigation: Check authorization, total costs, delivery, disputes, ownership and responsibility; use spending limits and human review when consequences cannot be reversed.
commerce.readerContext: Read all three due nodes and their source-dependent summaries, money tour and income links in both languages. The text introduces who receives money and separates revenue, profit and fulfillment.
commerce.whyHere: Advance the three substantively reread node dates, retain their prose and categories, and leave unchanged link and evidence-summary dates intact.

finance.mechanism: Financial AI use may contribute to correlated operations or abuse, but system-wide disruption also requires propagation through important functions and inadequate buffers or response.
finance.conditions: Reread the Bank of England 2024 survey’s executive findings and methodology, FSB’s 2024/2025 original summaries and the BIS FSI 2026 cyber-resilience abstract. Compare these scopes with all six due finance nodes.
finance.counterexample: The 118 survey responses and fully autonomous use-case share are not current market transaction shares. Shared providers do not ensure matching trades. A local breach or price fall need not disable payments or credit across the system.
finance.evidence: Retain F1/F2/F2a/F2b/F3/F4. The institutional sources describe adoption and vulnerabilities, not an observed AI-caused global financial crisis or measured success of every proposed safeguard.
finance.limits: No full FSB/BIS PDF reread, new market data analysis or quantitative crisis prediction is claimed. Policy recommendations are not demonstrated defensive effectiveness.
finance.mitigation: Keep authorization and transaction limits, independent reconciliation, capital/liquidity buffers, shared-provider recovery and alternate payment paths. Assess actual correlated actions and response times.
finance.readerContext: Read the six nodes, F1-F3/F3-F5, related diagrams, focus text and money tour in both languages. Liquidity, propagation and confidence loss are explained separately from price and abundance.
finance.whyHere: Substantively retain the six due-node explanations and advance only their dates. No new finance evidence warrants revised levels or stronger causal arrows.

context.mechanism: The surrounding navigation and explanations organize prerequisites and conditional outcomes rather than scoring progress toward inevitable catastrophe.
context.conditions: Read fourteen affected graph definitions, five routes, four focus entries, thirteen evidence summaries, nine news contexts and five stories in Japanese and English, plus all twenty-three affected connections.
context.counterexample: Different models succeeding in different settings do not establish a complete AND path. A survey belief is not adoption, a payment is not profit and local loss of control is not irreversible global harm.
context.evidence: The updated originals are compatible with the existing conditional labels and beginner-facing introductions. Reference changes trigger dependency fingerprints without requiring categorical or topological changes.
context.limits: This dependency check is not a new audit of every old source, every unaffected card or every historical review. Unchanged node-summary, route and source dates are not refreshed just because their fingerprints depend on changed nodes.
context.mitigation: Keep clear actor, access, supervision and distribution conditions. Preserve recovery paths, counterexamples and separate definitions of observation, test results, extrapolation and hypothesis.
context.readerContext: Read tour passages together with standalone details so direct entry and sequential reading both provide the necessary context. Existing glossary coverage suffices for these additions.
context.whyHere: Retain affected context after actual bilingual reading, and record coverage without claiming fresh empirical evidence for each navigation object.

provenance.counterexample: Today’s index has nineteen incident reports and three notices, with October 15 reports absent from yesterday’s recorded snapshot. provenance.evidence: Add eight sources, seven cards and seven bilingual node updates; rereview twenty-seven due nodes and nine due edges. Thirty node dates and four associated summary dates change; prior history is preserved.
provenance.limits: Search is bounded and cannot guarantee discovery of every silent correction. No independent data replication, proof execution, physical-device, browser-layout or production test is claimed.
